utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Pejkovic, as well. I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I followed your instructions and I did not contact anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Registry for P420 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, yesterday we stopped in this document, D420; it's the second report from the year 2000. And we stopped at the paragraph which says that through your work in the ground you established that there were 20.000 unregistered returnees between 1995 and 2000? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to move to another topic connected to this document, and therefore I would ask the Registry to open page 3D001268 in the Croatian version, and page 3D060131 in the English version. This chapter, Mr. Pejkovic, talks about the project of return from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina through the stability pact. Could you please tell us a few introductory sentences about the stability pact. What is meant by that?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we talk about the stability pact, we have to know that one of the more important tasks before this stability pact was to enable the return of all refugees and displaced persons to their homes. And the government, as a participant in all this process, is connected to that, implemented through the stability pact and in co-operation with the relevant countries - in this case these were Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia and Montenegro - all the procedures in order to enable the fastest possible and easiest possible return of everyone to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What were the factors connected with the stability pact? You mentioned the countries, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as well as Croatia. And then, of international institutions, who was present there as well?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were responsible for the activities were UNHCR and OSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It says here that a budget of 55 and a half million US dollars was proposed for the pact, and that the target group of returnees numbered 16.500 persons. They would be the user of that. And these were the persons who had submitted applications for return, whether to the office that you were employed at, through the UNHCR. And if we consider the ethnic composition of the returnees, what was it?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily, this was the return of Croats, also the return of Serbs, and the return of the Muslim, that is to say, the Bosniaks. All the three groups were returning. The Croats were returning to Bosnia and Herzegovina and so were the Muslim Bosniaks, whereas, the Serbs were returning to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And please tell us what were the results of this project of return by implementation of the stability pact?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The programme for the return and the return itself, through the stability pact was just a part of the overall return, and when we're talking about return, it's difficult to distinguish what was return through the stability pact. We did have target groups. However, people returned in other ways as well, not only people that we wanted to return and that we considered as target groups as the stability pact but other people as well. So that when this report was drafted, a significant number of displaced persons and refugees had already returned to their home, both in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] now I would like to show page 3D001290 in the Croatian version, that is to say, page 3D060605 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Pages we will see on the screen are the summary, talking about the returns to Republic of Croatia in a period of five years since the previous report from 1995 until this report from the year 2000. Do I draw proper conclusions, Mr. Pejkovic?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And it says here in the seconds paragraph that since the fall of 1995 until the 1st of May, 2000, the total number of those who returned to the Republic of Croatia was 244.350 displaced persons. Where does this data come from, Mr. Pejkovic?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the data on the number of persons who had the status of returnees. They were all registered at the government office, and they received their returnee card. We must know that since 1997 until the moment of this report in the year 2000 a system of monitoring was completely established so that it was not possible to have errors in the data, because each person had his or her identity card, and their movements were monitored as well as their status. So both the status and the place where they were within the Republic of Croatia or the fact that they returned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This figure of 244.350 returnees is then broken down into three items. So I would ask you to look at the data on the screen and briefly comment on them and tell us also where do the data come from.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figures expressed here were the result of the sums that were made relating to the number of returnees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it true that I see on my screen not the same text in B/C/S and English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's your screen, as mine it is, then you don't see the English text on the left side of the screen. And the proper page of the English text is, as I said, 3D060605.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. I don't think I have that page in that -- in this document. I have been looking for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the page in the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's the right page on the screen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There we are now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I can assist my learned colleague, I could give you my copy, if you wish; although it's the same as -- as shown on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: This is -- sorry. This is D420.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is D420, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have it on our screen now. The English translation, which is uploaded, consists of 53 pages. Which number in these 53 is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Mikulicic answers ... Mr. President, I -- the document that I have that was printed off within the last two weeks doesn't actually have that range. It has a 3D06 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to figure out when it was uploaded into the system, when that happened. I know something changed yesterday, but I didn't realize any of the text changed. I thought that was the end of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we move a bit up the English text so that we can see the number at the bottom of the page, a bit to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was uploaded yesterday, and we informed the parties on the record. If you open up e-court, that's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's now the second page which is uploaded. The second out of 18, which is now uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have found it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I just -- I need one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The old 53-page English original appears under number 3D060100; whereas, this 18-page is now 3D060604. And we are looking at 0605. And then the B/C/S original is uploaded under 3D001242 and is 64 pages. Just for our information, Mr. Mikulicic, the two English uploaded documents, 53 pages for the 0100 -- no, I'm making a mistake. No. It's right. 53 pages for the 0100 and 18 pages for the 0604, are they both covered by the original 3D001242?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we have translations split up in two parts, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't think I understood that last part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you look in e-court, source and attachments, we find three originals which is understandable because, at the time, they were already translated. I'm looking at the document details at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm sad and yet happy to report it is the system here. I don't have three; I only two sets of translations. But on the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, as uploaded in e-court, we have three originals. And that is caused by the fact that already at the time translations were prepared and distributed as the witness testified yesterday. That's at least how I understand it. Then we have a B/C/S original uploaded under 3D001242, a 64-page document. Last part of the document, mainly tables. Then we have two sets in English, 3D060100, and 3D060604. That's, at least, always the first page of the English. And we're now looking at the second page of this sequence found under 3D060604.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that now. If I could just make once comment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: This was something that was just put on the record; it's been updated yesterday by Mr. Kuzmanovic. There was no indication that was going to be used during the cross-examination [sic], which, Prosecution feels, that it would have been more proper to give us notice that, in fact, that part was going to be used. It didn't form, actually, the document as identified on the exhibit list originally because now it has been added to in terms of the translation. So just to put that on the record: I think it would have been proper to actually tell us it was going use, not just in passing that it has been updated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Although we informed the learned colleagues from the Prosecution office that we are going to use the document D420, which is obviously the part of this document. But any way ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejkovic, before the procedural issues that arose, I asked you to comment, for the benefit of the Bench and the parties, the items 1, 2, and 3, which are a breakdown of the total number of 244.350 returnees in the period of five years, those who returned to the Republic of Croatia. So could you please be so kind to briefly comment on these figures?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we drafted the reports, we always tried to break down the data into logical wholes. So the first group is the number of returnees who were primarily Croats and who returned to the areas liberated by the military and police operations Flash and Storm. The second category included the return to or from the Croatian Danube region on the basis of the Erdut Agreement on the peaceful reintegration of the Croatian Danube region. And the third category related to the return into the Republic of Croatia from Yugoslavia; that is to say, Serbia and Montenegro, and Bosnia and Herzegovina. When we talk about the return of displaced persons to the areas which were liberated during the operations Flash and Storm until the 1st of May, 2000, the number was 122.517 returnees --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I understood properly, these returnees were primarily Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And can I please have the transcript in front of me so that can I see the speed of my own speech. The second figure was a two-way return from the Croatian Danube region and into the Croatian Danube region where it is stated that, as part of this process, 31.717 returnees returned. They were mostly or almost only Serbs who went to other parts of Croatia and who had been accommodated in the Croatian Danube region. And, at the same time, 48.995 returnees returned to the Croatian Danube region; they were mostly Croats and some representatives of other ethnic groups. And then we also showed here the return to Croatia from Serbia and Montenegro and Bosnia and Herzegovina and the figure was 41.121 returnee. And we broke down this figure into two; namely, 23.147 persons returned in an organised manner with the support of our office and UNHCR; whereas the remaining number returned spontaneously, which means that they had been issued Croatian documents and returned to Croatia on their own. And, upon return to Croatia, they contacted our office and were given the returnee status.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the third category of returnees, when you talk about the ethnic composition, who were the members of this group?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were almost 100 per cent the returning Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, Mr. Pejkovic, it says that from a total of about 300.000 Croatian Serbs who left their homes after 1991, their homes in the Republic of Croatia, that is, a total of 72.838 persons returned from the Croatian Danube region, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that, according to the current number of requests for return filed to the office for refugees, there was still 14.020 persons waiting to return. Where does this data come from, Mr. Pejkovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, perhaps you could ask the witness -- this case is primarily about the Krajina, that -- Sector South. Can we see what - when we're talking about returnees - what is the percentage which returned to the Krajina, because I get the feeling that we always get the whole of the -- of the Croatian return programme without any breakdown in Krajina and other regions. Mr. Pejkovic, could you help us out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. When speaking of the returning Serbs, we must say that 95 per cent of them took place in the formally occupied territory, in the territory of the so-called Krajina as you said yourself. There were very few of them who returned to the areas which were free throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that, but focussing -- because I -- it -- it seems that we're talking not just about the Krajina region, well, let's say, around Knin, former Sector South, but we're talking about areas at quite a distance from that. Do you have a breakdown from specifically those returning to -- to the Krajina, the ... Perhaps I should say Sector South, because that's what we are -- the area, say, roughly, around Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these documents contain tables listing municipalities in which returnees were. But we never drafted such reports in which we would try to calculate the figures of returnees solely to the area of north, south, or west. In item 2, though, we had data on Sector South, at least partially, because that is, for the most part, the Danube region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I could assist with the next document that I want to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll hear --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the Registrar for D429.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, you will see a document which has already been admitted. It is the statistics of the returnees and returnee applications, which was put together in late 2006 by the office; that is to say, the administration for IDPs and refugees. I don't think you'll be able to get your bearings quickly on this page, but I wanted to draw your attention to the following, given His Honour's question, to the left column, which states the counties to which those people returned. From the county names, perhaps you can conclude which of those would fall within this -- the former Sector South. That is to say, Knin, Zadar, Sibenik, Split, as well as Lika. Please focus on the entry under the number 09 which is the Licko-Sinjska county. Next, the number 13 which is the Zadar county. Then 15, the Sibenik-Knin county. And 17, the Split-Dalmatia county. From the data put together by the office, can you conclude whether these figures would relate to the area of the Former Republic of Krajina or Sector South which is important for this case? Perhaps can you offer a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, other than it being fully leading to direct someone to just ask them to add up numbers, I don't think it adds much just to simply read from documents and have the person confirm that's what it says there. It's not -- it's leading; it's improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's not uncommon in this courtroom. If statistics were prepared and then to ask for an explanation to that, of course, we wouldn't expect the witness to reproduce the numbers. That, of course, would be practically impossible. But to assist us in understanding, I think, is not inappropriate. Therefore, the witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mikulicic, Your Honour, I authored this table. The data shown here refers to a certain date. We collated it so that we would be able to follow the rate of return at the level of each and every county for statistic purposes and to inform the public. There is another table containing sub-statistics, in which we can see each and every municipality per county. But in that case, that included actually hundreds of tables. And, as such, it would have been extraordinary to them published. Those who were interested in monitoring the returnee process could peruse them, nevertheless. Overall return was followed at the level of counties, municipalities, or locations, or settlements. Extracting individual pieces of information, one can clearly ascertain the number of returnees to certain areas within Sector South, Sector North, or Sector West.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejkovic, if we look at the statistics, we see in the upper part of the table the column "Minority Return," which is further split into three columns from the FRY, from the B and H, and from the Croatian Danubian region. These were the categories you referred to only a minute ago when you discussed the 2000 report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what we could see under categories 1, 2, and 3. In this table, it is simply stated by using different terminology. But it all boils down to the same thing. We have returnees, that is to say, former IDPs in the first column, which refer to mostly Croats. Next we have minority returns from three different directions. And, for practical purposes, these were mostly Serbs. The directions were the FRY, Bosnia-Herzegovina, or the Croatian Danubian region. The next column shows the total of the three sub-columns. The next column is the total number of returnees. What follows is the number of cases or applications which are still pending.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, let us try and clarify one thing, and I would kindly ask for your assistance in that. This Tribunal discusses the area of the former so-called Krajina. Statistically and legally and formally speaking, does such a category exist within the Croatian system?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If you were asked how to define or show data of return to that area alone, how would you be able to do that?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could clearly identify the settlements or municipalities which had been occupied. We followed the rate of return there as well. We would have to add up all of them to arrive at a final figure of returnees to that specific area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we are talking about the overall minority return, then it brings us to the total figure of 123.469 persons on -- or as of the 2nd of December, 2006. According to the methodology you used, can you tell us what the ethnicity was of the people included in this figure of minority number of returnees?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we are discussing the minorities, it is almost 100 per cent Serbs. Okay, well, there may be a few percentages less than that, because there were people in mixed marriages, but for practical purposes, that this was almost solely the return of Croatian citizens of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, you worked in the IDPs and refugees office for a number of years; you cooperated with various international organisations, NGOs, governmental organisations, the Croatian government, et cetera. Has any pressure ever been exercised upon you, which would try to impose different solutions to your otherwise professional obligations?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say to this Court that there was never any pressure exercised, or, rather, the only pressure I felt was the need for us do our job as quickly and as well as possible, so as to enable as many people to -- as many people as possible to return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Pejkovic. Since you headed the office, perhaps you can tell us whether the office policy ever included any kind of discrimination by ethnicity, religion, sex, or any other?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of the office was to enable all those IDPs and refugees who were put under our care to help them in the exercise of their religious and ethnic feelings and practices. We tried to do that for each and every single person. We never discriminated. We did, however, keep data pertaining to all the individual cases of people who provided us with information to be able to see how many Croats, Serbs, Ruthenians, Jews, Czechs, Slovaks, and all other ethnicities returned. That is to say, all the ethnicities who felt the results of the war, having been expelled from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pejkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no questions for the witness. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Mr. Carrier, this brings us to you. And, of course, we heard from you yesterday; you explained what problems you were facing. And you said that you would further consider whether you would be ready to crosses examine the witness or not after you had had time to look at certain matters. Could you inform the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm still getting information that D420 has additional parts that still haven't been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Simple question: Is every part of D420 translated as uploaded in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, although the parts are separated, as you can see in the e-court. But we -- in the meantime, we ask of the CLSS just to consolidate the translation in one part so that will be more useable, not departed in three different partition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently the information is not the same. Mr. Carrier, what portions of D420 are missing at this moment, as far as translation is concerned? Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the entire document has been translated and uploaded. What is the specific issue about D420 that is causing the problem; and if we can answer that, we would be more than happy to help. But we added the additional translation of the document, which was already an exhibit, was translated in full, and uploaded. There is -- of D420. I keep mis-transposing [sic]; I'm sorry. So the issue is: What is the issue about D420 that causes an issue for the Prosecution? And we -- if we can answer that, we will help. Otherwise, we don't really know what the issue is, other than part of it wasn't translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I was first asking Mr. Carrier what the information exactly was that not every portion of D420 was translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I was simply just passed a note saying that one of the people on our team has indicated that it is still not complete, and we need to just check it. But the issue is raised; if Mr. Kuzmanovic isn't aware. We raised them yesterday as well that there are still numbers from April 2000 document, and there's numbers from May 2005, and we were given now an additional 18 pages yesterday which was - as I stated already on the record - it was put in without identifying that that was going to be referred. There is more tables; there's numbers. These things all need to be properly looked at in order to cross-examine the witness. Particularly now that he has been asked questions about it during the -- in chief at the end on new portions. But we're not confident that the actual translation that was uploaded originally, the initial 49 pages, is actually a translation of what the B/C/S is. I think it was an English version that was found and was put in as -- as the translation, to stand for the translation, but not a true translation of what the B/C/S document was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But in order to further explore these problems, Mr. Carrier, you will have to guide us to say, Well, that's what we finds here; that's what we find there; this is not consistent; or this is not a translation. Although it looks like -- I mean, passing messages that matters are incomplete, of course, do not immediately guide us to the solution. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would add that we've had 24 hours since this issue was raised or more. We've exchanged I don't know how many e-mails with the OTP related to other witness lists and exhibit lists and scheduling. And not one e-mail was sent to us asking us to either clarify this or give us some more information or it's not complete. We would have been more than happy to assist, but we didn't get any information in the interim time-frame that there was a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you were aware of the problems the OTP expressed yesterday. But, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: It was addressed partly in the filing, Your Honour. But if you turn to page 32, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 32 from what, exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry. For the initial English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The initial English translation. Let me see whether I -- we are talking about D420.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, it's 3D--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, then I'll get it on my screen. Okay. Which consists of three originals, one in English, two in -- two in English, one in B/C/S. Which page in the B/C/S version you would like us to look at?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry. It's 35 in the English. I'm just going look up the B/C/S version. I think it's 3D0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you say it's not translated, then we start with what seems to be the most original, that is, the Croatian version first. utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just point out one thing. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: Your Honour, I just need one moment.

utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, would you agree that where you drew our attention to missing portions of a translation, that if would you take these two parts together, that it seems to be a complete translation?

utterances.text: Then please take us to a part which is not translated or not fully translated.

utterances.text: Yes. utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll let -- go ahead and finish, and I'll address --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then, if there's other document, please inform the Registrar so that we have hard copies of those available as well. So that we can work on it. Because now I'm manipulating my screen, which goes well, but I am losing oversight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the database, Mr. Waespi informed me yesterday that the database has been located, and it will be given to us in terms of a disclosure. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give you an opportunity to answer, let's -- Mr. Misetic, is back in his seat again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, there were three issues. The first, portions of D420 missing in translation.

utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. If -- the first point, I know Mr. Misetic found a part of the document before. And just to explain the situation, that was what was added in a translation yesterday without notifying us that -- that that's where parts of the report were coming from. And just to be clear, that was what we objected to. We filed an objection to the statement on Friday. And the report -- the updated translation was put in without telling us, Oh, by the way the -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But since yesterday you knew, and since yesterday we thought that you would seek what -- how you could resolve these matters. But, yes, okay. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And so if you start looking at -- if you pull up the English version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: English version of --

utterances.text: -- of D420 and go to page 3D060109; and that's section 3.3. And in Croatian, 3.3 starts on page 3D001252.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, if you could just -- Mr. Registrar, if you could just align the 3.3 part. And if we begin counting the paragraphs and we just turn the page -- I mean, again, I think the problem is that this isn't a translation, it's just an English version and a Croatian version. But if you count the paragraphs, the first few seem to line up, for the first six, any way, until, I think, it gets down to -- If you could turn the page in English and the B/C/S, please. Right. You can see there's no 3.4 there. I think data on return might just be -- I don't know if that's above number 3, which is in Croatian "adresa povratka." And then it goes into 3.4. If you keep going through the section, you can see these don't line up. And so obviously not speaking or reading Croatian, it's hard to tell where these are coming from. So if you keep moving --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, let's take it one by one. 3.3, Mr. Carrier tell us that in the beginning it looks more or less the same; and then, at a certain moment, he says it becomes pretty different. utterances.text: Your Honour, during the break, I had a contact with Office of the Prosecutor with Mr. JJ du Toit. And obviously in Croatian version of the document which was uploaded into the e-court --

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: That is to say, that the -- the both versions were original, English and Croatian. utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mikulicic, let me first be very candid with you. I mean, giving two different versions; and I do not see what the problem is. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no problem with that, That -- the fact that there are a couple pages missing. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, if you don't speak that other language, and if you have to find your way through it, and then to say that these really minor page numbering at the bottom, that that should immediately be the clue to resolution of the problem, let's -- the work done by the Defence was sloppy, and Mr. Carrier is entitled to make these observations and should now not be blamed for -- It would have been better, perhaps, to contact, Mr. Carrier, let me -- But to -- that you blame him for that, if the Chamber would do that it would be different. utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not confident that that's the case given -- this is not a translation; it's just an English version that was created. By who, I don't know. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, I think I gave you already such support that to seek even more seems to be a bit over-asking.

utterances.text: Well, as I said before, we actually had disclosed these already to the Defence. We told them that yesterday; they're in their lockers. It has been given to them. I'm hearing noises. utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: If it were -- if it were you could determine certain numbers to double-check the numbers being in the statement or being produced in Exhibit D420, for example. utterances.text: Yeah. Third issue we left you with before the break was the contacts with the -- between OTP and this witness.

utterances.text: So to say that your information is that if it had been discussed, then it would have been in such a general way and not focussed concretely on this witness to be called by the Prosecution.

utterances.text: Well, if the English is a translation of the original. If it is not, then it should have been translated.

utterances.text: Yes. That is disclosure at this moment. And two - I have to ask these days - is it 2.00 a.m. or 2.00 p.m., Mr. Carrier?

utterances.text: Sorry, it was 2.00 p.m., 1400.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That comes as a relief to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.text: I stand corrected, Your Honour, it was -- e-mail was sent at 2.12 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC

utterances.text: Did you work with -- you worked with Mr. Sterc, though, right?

utterances.text: And you've never read this statement that Mr. Sterc gave that was submitted to the Tribunal?

utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could ask that you call onto the screen Exhibit D1607. This is the witness statement from Mr. Sterc. And if we can just stay with the English translations. And if I can put, next to that, on the other screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm just looking at the Prosecutor's exhibit list, and it's not -- I don't see D1607 on that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if is not on there, I apologise. It was just an oversight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, having heard the explanation or at least an answer to your question, what -- you're still on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, no. I'm just -- actually, I'm scrolling down, Mr. President, to see if I can see it described or misnumbered in some fashion, but I didn't see it. But, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you listen to -- yes, Mr. Carrier leaves it open that it has been a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I apologise. It doesn't seem to be on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see any application for the Chamber to stop you, so, therefore, proceed, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, I appreciate it, Mr. President. And if we could have Mr. Pejkovic's statement on the screen, which is D1825. And if we go to page 5 in Mr. Pejkovic's statement, which is -- for people following along in the B/C/S, it's page 5 as well. And in Mr. Sterc's statement, if we could go to paragraph 14 in the English, which is on page 9, which is page 8 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, I just want to highlight a part of your statement, which starts at the bottom of paragraph 14, and then goes on to paragraph 15. And I want to compare that to paragraph 14 of Mr. Sterc's statement. And then I will ask you a question. At the bottom of paragraph 14, in respect of the Programme for Return and care of expelled person, refugees, and displaced persons which is, I believe, D428. This is what you said: "The most important document" -- that this was "the most important document of the Working Group." And if we look at paragraph 14 of Mr. Sterc's statement. He says: "This programme was the most important document of the Working Group." And into part -- paragraph 15 of yours, you mention that: "The Assembly of the Republic of Croatia adopted it without any votes of abstention or votes against." And then a bit further on, you say: "The UN Security Council came out in favour of the programme as well." And if we compare that to Mr. Sterc, in paragraph 14, he says: "The Croatian parliament accepted the same unanimously with no votes against or undecided." And he goes on to say: "The programme was reviewed positively by practically everybody and even by the UN Security Council." And down a bit further in your paragraph 15, Mr. Pejkovic, you said: "The repatriation programme covered practically all aspects of the repatriation process actions to be undertaken by all subjects involved in the return, the authority of all institutions, the duties of all parties, the repatriation and reconstruction, financing methods, the time-limits, the priorities, the return of property, the care for all who could not return to other states, et cetera, and the setting up of a commission for its execution." And then, at the end of paragraph 15, you said: "The programme continues being implemented to this day, with minority changes." And if you look at paragraph 14 of Mr. Sterc's statement, he said: "The programme was implemented until today with some minority changes. The programme defined nearly all segments of return and reconstruction" -- sorry, "of return, the competency of the institutions, obligations on all sides, financing of the return and reconstruction, deadlines, priorities, return of property, accommodation for all those who cannot return to other countries, et cetera, and the establishment of the commission for its implementation." And I'm told that, actually, the -- some of the words or sentences are actually identical in the middle of paragraph 14 to what you have. And, Mr. Pejkovic, I'm just wondering if you're suggesting that the wording in the order of presentation in this part of the statement we just looked at from yours and Mr. Sterc, are you saying that's just a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that we relied on the same documents when we used the option of copy and paste. When I compare the two texts, both statements represent a compilation of the documents we have been discussing today. That is to say, the 1995 report, the 2005 report, and the programme of return itself that was adopted by the Croatian parliament and published as such in the Official Gazette on the 7th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, I did ask you if you -- your statements were in your own words, and you said yes. So are you saying now that you were cutting and pasting out of different documents to put together a statement and so you're not actually using your own words. Is that what you're telling us now?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I formulated my document, relying on the existing documents. And that is the method I used to provide my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I actually understand what that means. Does that mean that your statement is simply just a compilation of different pieces of different documents. It's not really a statement; it's just a cut-and-paste job from a bunch of, I'm presuming, Croatian documents?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand why you believe it not to be my statement. This is my statement. However, the way I went about it may be a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So did you just -- you typed something up or cut and pasted something and handed it over to the Defence and said, Here's my statement, or were you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first drafted a more extensive body of text or material that we used subsequently to draft the statement, which I signed in front of one of the attorneys of the Defence team of General Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, yesterday you were asked some questions about the methodology employed to produce some of the numbers that you're relying on in your statement. When you were asked specifically about methodology, I think you said data processing from database. Can you explain the exact name of the statistical programme that you were running to produce the numbers, and also give us a sense of the degree or margin of error calculated for the numbers being produced by your system?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used a Unix engine with an installed recital base. Data was entered and then processed by the programme itself. So, since you're asking me about the statistical margin of error, I'll tell you this: If you have a -- your current account in the bank, you are aware that at any given time the programme can produce a piece of information which not necessarily -- which does not necessarily reflect the data in the database. The results shown here are based on the information from the database. Therefore, I believe them to be 100 per cent correct. The only error may be in the software itself, in the programme. But, with time, if one corrects such glitches, then a programme of that kind always produces the same result.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, you're talking about controlling or adjusting for glitches in the programme. I'm asking for other potential pieces of error. So I will be specific: human error; so, data input, degree of incomplete forms filled in, degree of error from duplicated input, degree of error for incomplete key stroke. You -- did you account for all that, and can you give us the specific numbers on how you calculated that degree of error?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By profession, I'm an IT specialist. I was in charge of data processing for a large bank. In this process, I used the best of my knowledge and abilities to organise data processing along the same lines by the governmental office for IDPs and refugees. For any access to the database, files were kept to see what terminal was used to enter the database, who did it, under what authority, and what field that person checked, updated, edited or deleted within the database. In the process of data entry, of course, there may be data which is either incorrectly recorded in the field or incorrectly entered in the field; and, as such, through the process of data processing, such pieces of information are detected; and, as such, cannot be entered into the database until such time that they are corrected. It is only, as such, that they can be entered into the database. In other words, the database contents are 100 per cent correct and reflect the situation in the documents. The results of the database can be searched according to certain predetermined algorithms, when, for example, we order a selection of all syllables in the names of all returnees who returned to the area of the Sibenik Knin county, until, say, the 1st of May, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- such result would say be --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... getting -- that part's too complicated. That wasn't part of my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, you interrupted at a moment when the witness's words had not been finished and not been translated yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I apologise. I was just trying to stop. It was going into information that wasn't responsive to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But they are, Your Honour, by all means. I mean, it is our position that one could not ask a questions and not to allow the witness do answer that questions, whatever the answer could be complicated or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was how the witness calculated the degree of errors. You may finish your answer. At the same time, could you please focus on detection of errors, rather than to describing the whole system. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the data presented, there is no error. All errors must be detected and corrected before the data enters the database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, in your statement you indicated that 8.000 Serbs had left during Operation Flash. Could you just confirm that you're talking about the operation that happened, beginning of May 1995?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: You also state that during Operation Storm, 120.000 Serbs left Croatia. Now, Mr. Pejkovic, if -- I'm going ask you to look at document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If could I have Exhibit P644 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps meanwhile, I can ask one additional question to you, Mr. Pejkovic. We're talking about the database. On from what moment you consider that the database, as you just described as being infallible, more or less, was functioning? I mean, from what date you consider that you were working with a database which would detect all errors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The database which made it impossible for errors to be entered because there is correlation and cross-reference between the pieces of information, because the software would not allow erroneous pieces of information, the database, as such, operated from 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you this because you say, Well, whatever mistake there was, the database would detect that. Now, I do understand that if you try to give some input so as to say that a person is both a man and a woman, then, of course, the system would immediately detect that. But we saw yesterday, we saw figures where you told us that they had to be corrected by one third, I remember, over 100.000, because the situation on the ground did not match with the figures that were -- were in the database at that time. Therefore, when you say that errors would be detected, that would be certain kind of errors that would be detected by the system. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. There were errors before 1995. As I have tried to explain yesterday, that was the reason why we created new lists which partially were there because of the errors made back in 1992 and 1993, as well as 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday you said that these errors could not any further occur since 1997 because then you had the system with the individual documents. But do I have to understand your answer now that, already from 1995, no such errors could be made anymore in this system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Looking at this exhibit, P644, which is a report dated 18 October 1995 to the UN General Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And if we can turn to paragraph 8 and 9 in the English, which should be on page -- starting on page 3 in the English, I think. And turn to the same in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, here the UN is reporting that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but the Croatian version on the right hand of the screen is not -- it's not matching with the English one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now it is. At least for paragraph 8. I don't know what part you wanted to quote from the original, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: The UN is reporting that 12.000 Serbs left Croatia, as a result of Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, could you always tell us where to find it on a page, because we try to follow you. Where do we say? Which paragraph are we in?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I apologise. It's paragraph 8, and it says in the beginning, and I'll just read: "On May 1st, 1995, the Croatian Army launched a military offensive in the area of Western Slavonia known as Sector West." And then turning to the next -- the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pejkovic, you indicated that this is -- what you said was Operation Flash. And if you look at paragraph 9, it gives a number of figures, and it's saying that roughly - if you look at the different figures - that roughly 12.000 Serbs left Croatia as a result of that operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If I just be a little bit more precise. It says 10.000 civilians and military personnel in the first line. So I -- I don't know if we're talking about people or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier said that the UN was reporting that 12.000 Serbs left Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He apparently, although it was -- he didn't make it easy for us to follow him because he was quoting from not the page which was on the screen, but we now finally found that page. He did not make any distinction between civilian or military. He just said Serbs. And that's -- that is still to be seen whether we find that in paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's in beginning of paragraph 9, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, does it say Serbs there? It says over -- Mr. Carrier, if would you please introduce these matters in an organised way, that is, step by step, that is, not to say slowly, but to say, Let's look at this report, where the UN describes so and so and so; in paragraph 9 we find the numbers. I do not see anything, but it could be the context of paragraph 8 that these are Serbs. It doesn't say so. And then a further 2.000 Croatian Serbs decided to leave in the following weeks. That makes approximately 12.000. Serbs. Just that. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So, just looking at those numbers, if we can now turn to -- and just keep those in mind, Mr. Pejkovic. If we could turn to paragraph 13, which says that in the early hours of 4 August 1995 the Croatian Army launched a major military offensive against the Krajina region in the course of the -- and then turning the page in English. The following days it established control of the whole of Sectors North and South. Approximately 200.000 of the Krajina Serb inhabitants, or 95 per cent of the population of the two sectors, fled into Bosnian Serb-held areas in western Bosnia and most continued their flight to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro)." Now, Mr. Pejkovic, I'm just wondering, given your numbers, can you count for the discrepancy between the numbers in your statement and those that were being reported to the United Nations General Assembly in October 1995, specifically the fact that you're indicating that roughly 80.000 fewer Serbs fled in the wake of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. But could we have a distinction between the previous figures, which refers to 10.000 civilian and military personnel? Which part is military personnel, and which part is civilian personnel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You cannot compare two figures which are not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then hear from the witness, or you can deal with the matter in re-examination. The UN report doesn't make that distinction, and this witness is certainly able to -- if there's anything wrong in the question, he will certainly identify that. And if not, let's try to -- not to interrupt the flow of evidence too easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try to minimise my interruption, Your Honour. But it's not fair to the witness. You have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... we have do tell witness that the comparison is not the same. So my learned colleague could also talk about the Macedonians who left, I don't know, some other portion of Croatia. So it is not the same. So how can you compare the two things which are not the same? I simply cannot understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you can. But let's -- Mr. Carrier, you are now aware that -- and please understand that the Chamber, keeping control over these matters, sees the documents now and has to immediately find out, on the one hand side, Mr. Carrier should be able to go on. At the same time, could you be very precise in your question as what to compare. Give the exact sources and the quotes so that we know what we are comparing, Mr. Carrier. You said you referred to the -- I think it was -- let me check. Let's, again, look at your question. You want the witness to compare the number of 12.000 Serbs leaving what area exactly, Mr. Carrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, I just -- I pointed out, first, his two -- he gives two numbers in the statement at paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So if you -- that's an organised way. Then you take him to paragraph 7, you said. He gives, there, numbers being --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... sorry, Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Paragraph 7, I mistakenly presumed that -- and I should have just pointed out to the Chamber, but he says 8.000 Serbs left during Operation Flash. And he also says that 120 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: -- during Storm. I apologise. I did say in the beginning of the question that in his statement he said that, but I didn't point to the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so we have now ... he gives an estimate of 8.000 Serbs leaving Croatia during Operation Flash and leaving Croatia; and 120.000 Serbs leaving Croatia during Operation Storm. 90.000 civilians, 30.000 members of Serb forces. It says "paramilitary." Now, what would you like the witness to compare this with?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, my question was, and I can read it again: Can you count for the discrepancy between the numbers in his statement, in relation to those two operations, and, in this report, to the United Nations General Assembly in October 1995. And I asked him to specifically consider the fact that he said that roughly 80.000 fewer Serbs fled in the wake of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So that is what I was asking him to explain, in terms of these numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that was during Operation Storm, after the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And just generally in terms of the numbers that he is giving to the UN that I just quoted to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you explain why the UN says that -- no, it says that 200.000 Krajina Serb -- Serbs, 95 per cent of the two sectors with are -- which are, at this moment, Mr. Carrier, were Sectors North and South.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, north and south.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: North and south fled into Bosnian Serb-held areas in western Bosnia. So what you would say is the number is far higher as reported by the UN, for Sectors North and South, as it is in the report of this witness, 120.000 during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Statement of the witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: The numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, both are estimates: the estimates of the UN and the estimates of the Croatian government, as to the numbers of population that was present in these areas and how many people left the areas. And that is all I can answer to this question. The numbers never corresponded; we never agreed about them. And history has shown that when, later on, one looks at the data that UNHCR was using, that the figures are closer to the estimates that we made than the ones that the UN made at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Pejkovic, you were aware that international observers were coming up with different numbers from what you, as members of the Croatian government, were explaining, in terms of the number of Serbs that had left?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, the figures provided by the UN were their estimates. They never conducted a census of the population nor did they have the data relating to the demographic movements. But somebody just said 200.000 and that was the number that was used all the time. But it was not supported by anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: The Croatian government wasn't running a census of the number of Serbs that were fleeing at the time of Operation Storm or in the aftermath of Operation Storm, were they?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And it could not run such a census. But it did list all those who had remained. And it ran a census, and the fact is that 10.000 people - the elderly, the frail, the weak - remained in the area and immediately they started providing assistance to this population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, were you ever aware of the fact that senior Croatian authorities or anybody in the government was lying about the number of Serbs that returned after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, I'm not aware that anyone lied. My office published the data on the return. Now, how somebody may have interpreted the data, I cannot answer about that. But I know what we, as the office, reported to the government and the Croatian public.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have Exhibit 2589 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Pejkovic, what you are going to see on the screen is a transcript dated 25 October 1995 of a meeting held between President Tudjman. Other people that were present included Minister Susak, Minister Jarnjak, Mr. Kostovic; there was other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 15 in the English and 17 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the page, where you have Mr. Jarnjak speaking -- and just for context - and my friends, I'm sure, will correct me if I'm misstating this - but the topic of discussion or one of the general topics of discussion here is the return of Serbs to Croatia, which goes from basically page 15 and 16. And this is what Mr. Jarnjak said --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If we could get the right page in the B/C/S, please, so that the witness and the Defence can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... sorry, I said page 17. Sorry, maybe it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can see that it's at the bottom of the page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If it's -- sorry, I -- it may be that the -- Minister Jarnjak shows up at the bottom of 15 and 17. Maybe my friend can direct me. It's the words -- it starts: "I will issue a task tomorrow."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the last sentence at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Is that, sorry, 15 or 17?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Minister Jarnjak, he says: "I will issue a task tomorrow to see how many have already been returned, one part has" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: "... one part has been returned, and we have returned some of those humanitarian problems. Therefore, I think there are already a couple of hundred who are exactly that family reunion. We will then publish and say yes to such politics, that method of family reunion but individual cases, no mass return." Then Dr. Kostovic relies: "I have lied that a couple of thousand have already arrived, so this has to be do carefully because it might provoke ..." Then he gets cut off. Now you just said there was interpreting. But it's -- you'll agree with me that it's clear that Mr. Kostovic is talking about lying about the number of Serbs that have returned; it's not just an interpretation of numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt, Your Honour. But what is following from that discussion is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, yes, but Mr. -- no, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This question can be put to the witness; the witness can read it; And how to interpret it, next line is also -- let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But it has to do -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, Mr. -- any objection to this question is -- as far as you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's concern of Bosnia, Your Honour, not on Croatia. Jajce town is in Bosnia. So what has to do with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if -- I was going to tell Mr. Kehoe to make the same objection. If Mr. Carrier wants to suggest the context of this is, as is phrased in the question he put, then I think he needs to establish more foundation as to what number this relates to, which group. What the lie relates to, which group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's read the context. Mr. Carrier, I would have to have the previous page again, and I would like the witness to read the whole of the previous page, so as the context to be established by himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the subsequent paragraph I think is also -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we start with what was before that. And we, in English, also, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: In English, I think if you -- if you start reading, perhaps, from page 13, Minister Jarnjak says: "They all phone every day." Your Honour, the lead-up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking myself whether we have exactly the same ... Could we -- for me, without having the full oversight. It's extremely difficult to know exactly where the witness should start reading. Mr. Carrier, it's clear that context is, in view of the two Defence teams, is very relevant. Without any further comment, could you tell the witness where he should start reading so as to have the full context of what you're asking questions about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, sorry, I believe on -- in English, I'm not really sure what they're referring to. In English there is a lead-up starting with Minister Jarnjak where they say: "They all phone every day." And they talk about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "They all phone..." Who's "they"?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, then he mentions a name, and it goes on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no I understand. But if I say "they phone," is there any context which explains who "they" are? And we are at which page out of 36 where the phone -- let's me just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, what was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "They" phoning, is which page out of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, I said before. It's at page 13 of 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And then he mentions somebody who is a member of, apparently, the Sabor, a Serb. They start talking about different lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, just for clarity. One from Ambassador Galbraith. I don't think he was the ambassador to Bosnia at the time. That's the context that they were considering, in Bosnia, they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it looks as if we're talking about - and please correct me when I'm wrong. I take it from Kostovic's remarks, the first one's appearing on page 13 that we're talking about. People in Belgrade who request their return.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's now clear. And then -- Is that clear to you, Mr. Pejkovic, that people phoning are apparently those who are in Belgrade and who want to return? Could you, then, please read from page -- and the -- Could you guide us as far as the B/C/S is concerned? Because, apparently, it's not, at this moment -- yes, could you assist Mr. -- Yes, I see that -- could you please read from the bottom of the page which is now on your screen, where the number of 50 appears? Then could we move to the next page. Mr. Pejkovic, if you have finished reading that page, please tell us so that we move to the next one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have read this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please move to the next one. Have you read that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for the parties next time, they're invited to ask the Chamber to ask the witness to read certain portions for purposes of context rather than to -- becoming emotional. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what I did say, originally, that was -- basically the discussion was return of Serbs to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And you see my question was, in relation to something you had said in your prior testimony, that maybe the numbers were about interpretation. And I'm saying, having read that, you see that it's not just interpretation. Mr. Kostovic says he has actually been lying about the number of Serbs that have returned. Are you able to say -- do you have any comment on that? Or are you aware of any other Serb officials -- or, sorry, Croatian government officials not being honest about the numbers that actually returned?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on specific persons and what they expressed or said and whether this person was telling the truth or not. I can only comment on a part which we have read. And I said yesterday that we did receive these requests for return from Ambassador Galbraith, as well as from the office in Belgrade; and that, as mentioned here, we resolved them through family reunion, so on humanitarian grounds. And there was no return en masse, because, at that moment, no agreement had been signed. Diplomatic ties had not been re-established with Serbia so that the organisation of a return en masse would be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: In paragraph 11 of your statement, Mr. Pejkovic, you state that up until May 1996 the ODPR had processed 5.895 repatriation requests of those who had fled during Storm and Flash. And you saw what we just read, and you said that had you lists from Ambassador Galbraith as well as the office in Belgrade et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And if we could please have Exhibit P1102 on the screen, which is a June 1996 report. And the subject is the refugee census in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph you see -- or in the first paragraph it's about a report that's attached to this document. And there's a view that the picture that is emerging is the very slow return of refugees to the areas in which they join a majority and the non-return of refugees to areas they will constitute a minority is very worrying.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And if we turn the page in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And under the heading of "Return," in the second paragraph, there's a number of -- numbers of people that want to return - I can go through them here. It says that 32.000 Croatian Serbs registered for return to the Human Rights Helsinki Committee in Belgrade, which is an organisation you mentioned yesterday during your testimony. That registration started in August 1995, which is an ongoing process. That the UNHCR - which is said UNHRC here - 20.000 of these applications were forward to the US Embassy in Zagreb with the idea that the US Embassy could apply some pressure to the Croatian government. Next then in the next paragraph down it says: "Approximately 22.000 Croatian Serbs sheltered in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia following the fall of the Krajina have applied to the Croatian bureau in Belgrade to return." Now, comparing these numbers of people applying to return - you've already mentioned you got lists from Ambassador Galbraith, et cetera - can you explain why a relatively small number of return requests had been processed by your office as of May 1996?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The text says: "Resolved."

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... resolved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Can you explain -- first off, can you explain what "resolve" means, and why, relative to the numbers we just went through in this document, why that is a relatively small number?

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reading this material, what I stated in my statement is just confirmed; namely, that, on the basis of humanitarian family reunion, reuniting family members, it says here that we resolved the issue of 8.000 persons in this document. And in my statement it says that at around this time we received applications from about 30.000 persons, that around 16.000 persons were interested in return, and around 14.000 persons had stated certain political conditions. That is to say, concern conditions in connection with their property. Of the 16.000 who expressed their wish to return, not all fell within this category whose situation would be resolved, on the basis of humanitarian family reunion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I think that you basically recited paragraph 9 in answer to that. But can you explain what you mean by "resolve"? And do you have a number of -- for those cases that you resolved, how many of those people actually returned? And to be specific, we're focussing on paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "resolved" means that on the basis of a request, a paper, an approval was issued, an approval for the return to the Republic of Croatia. We could not monitor everyone at the time, whether they, indeed, returned; and, therefore, in our data, we often mentioned, as my report also says, that around 20.000 persons was the estimate of those who were not registered and that these were the Serb returnees.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If they weren't registered, how would have you any idea of how many there were? Because your office, the ODPR, was only dealing with people who were registered as a displaced person or a refugee.

utterances.speaker: LOVRE PEJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report, you can see the data: how many applications were filed, how many were resolved, and how many persons did return. I do not have the report in front of me, so I cannot say off the top of my head anything about the data. But you can show them on the screen, and then I can repeat all that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I may assist to my learned colleague, this is a document 420, page 3D001248 in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this might be a good time for a break. I'm ready to move on to the next section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, if the witness wants to consult any of his reports in answering your questions, it would assist if you would give him an opportunity to do so. But it could be done after the break as well. We have a break, and we resume at ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I just wanted to raise an issue before we start. I don't think I will be able to finish today, given the slow process. And I apologise. I estimated two sessions. I don't know if I'll even -- by the of today whether I would have used two sessions, but I don't think I will finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Try to do your best, Mr. Carrier. And we will see what happens. By the way, I think that -- well, order in the courtroom is, of course, always required. But intellectual order, in the minds of those who are examining and are objecting, certainly would also assist in gaining time. I mean, if you put a question clearly saying, This is where we start, that -- that -- rather than, et cetera, and moving to -- and the same is true for some of the objections. Let's try to keep our mind disciplined. I'll try to do the same and hope that I will manage. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.
